One of the first complaints presented to doctors by many people later diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease is an involuntary tremor or shaking of the hands, fingers, arms, legs, jaw, and face. You’re most likely to notice this tremor when your hands are at rest rather than when you’re using them, although you may see more tremors while your hands and arms are in use as the disease progresses.  There are many causes of tremors. Parkinson's Disease is one of the most common causes, and tremors are often the first sign of the disease. The tremor and other symptoms may initially appear only on one side of the body, or they may appear worse on one side than the other. A repetitive “pill-rolling" movement between the thumb and finger—named because it looks as though the person is rolling a pill between their fingers—is characteristic of a Parkinsonian tremor. Some symptoms of Parkinson's are caused by the larger symptom of slowed movements (also known as bradykinesia). This primarily affects motor functions from walking and balance to writing and even motor functions that are often considered reflexive or spontaneous.  These slowed movements are a very common early sign of Parkinson’s, and may show up at the onset of the disease in 80% of patients. Some people might have a hard time describing what they are feeling and use words like “weakness,” “tiredness,” or “incoordination” when talking about these symptoms. Look for distortions in voluntary movements. In addition to involuntary movements, those with Parkinson’s may experience disturbances in their voluntary movements beyond just slowness. Some of the treatments used for Parkinson's disease may cause abnormal involuntary movements, or an increase in movement, referred to as dyskinesia. These distortions (dyskinesias) can be similar to a “tic” in appearance and worsen with psychological stress. Advanced dyskinesia is most often seen in patients who have been on the medication Levodopa for some time. A common symptom of Parkinson’s is a shuffling gait with short steps and a tendency to lean forward. People with Parkinson's often have difficulty with their balance, and there is sometimes a tendency to fall forward, causing the person to walk faster and faster to keep from falling over. This pattern is called a "festinating gait," and it is very common in Parkinson's disease. This symptom typically shows up in the later stages of the disease. Those with Parkinson’s Disease often lean forward at the waist when standing or walking. This is because Parkinson's can cause posture and balance problems, including rigidity. There is a tendency to flex the arms and the head so that the person appears bent over with the elbows flexed and the head down.  Rigidity can affect the whole body, and might you feel stiff or sore. Check for postural rigidity. Also referred to as “cog-wheeling,” this symptom presents as a hallmark, rigid motion when an examiner moves the arm of a patient through basic flexion and extension motions. The rigidity and resistance to movement is most obvious with passive movement of the wrists and elbow. Cog-wheeling may happen when the increased muscle tone related to rigidity is combined with a tremor. Some cognitive impairment is common, but usually not until late in the course of the disease. Around 90% of those with PD will show signs of speech disturbances at some point. These can present as quieter speech, breathy or hoarse qualities to the voice, and reduced precision with language. The voice often becomes soft or whispery because the vocal muscles lack mobility. Up to 60% of those with PD may show signs or anxiety or depression. PD affects some of the mood-stabilizing portions of the brain, which leads to this increased chance for depression, especially paired with the quality of life for patients in late stages of the disease. The muscles used to push food through the digestive system are also affected by PD. This can lead to a variety of gastrointestinal issues from incontinence to constipation. These same symptoms often present along with difficulty swallowing food as well. Many of the involuntary movements associated with Parkinson’s make it increasingly difficult for those with the disease to get a full night of sleep. Other symptoms—such as muscle rigidity making it difficult to roll over at night or bladder issues leading to getting up at night to urinate frequently—compound the sleep disruptions experienced by those with PD.

They can form anywhere on a guinea pig’s body, but the most common locations are the head and neck.  An abscess in the neck could be a swelling of the lymph node in that area. Lymph nodes are small glands that help the body fight infection. An abscess can feel firm or soft. Abscesses can also form in the mouth or jaw of a guinea pig. Abscesses in these areas can become large very quickly. Your guinea pig may look fine on one day, then have a large abscess the next day. When you handle your guinea pig, gently open its mouth to see the abscess. If the abscess is in the jaw, you will see a large bump along your guinea pig’s jawline. Guinea pigs can get several types of cysts, with the most common being a sebaceous cyst. Sebaceous cysts contain oil from the skin glands that produce oil (sebaceous glands). Sebaceous cysts are typically located on a guinea pig’s back and near the rump, but can form in other places as well. Although they can become very large, cysts are usually about the size of a pea. Cysts become a problem if they become large. Tumors can also form lumps. For example, a lump on your guinea pig’s tail could indicate a skin tumor called trichofolliculoma.  A lump on the chest could indicate another type of cancer called lymphosarcoma.  A female guinea pig can develop a mammary tumor, which you would see as a lump on the belly.  Lipomas are tumors made up of fat cells. There are no specific places where you would look for a lipoma on your guinea pig. Your guinea pig may have several lipomas at one time. Sometimes, a lump can make a guinea pig feel so bad that it doesn’t want to eat. For example, if your guinea pig is not eating its meals and doesn’t want any tasty treats, check its mouth for an abscess. Even if your guinea pig wants to eat, the size of the abscess in its mouth or jaw could make it difficult to chew food. Arbitration clauses. They sound innocuous enough. But, in a three part-series about clauses buried in tens of millions of contracts, Jessica Silver-Greenberg and Michael Corkery (along with another reporter, Robert Gebeloff) reported on the way these clauses have deprived Americans of one of their most fundamental constitutional rights: their day in court.

Read by millions, the series shows how arbitration clauses contained in most contracts — like employment, telephone service, credit cards — have crept into nearly every corner of Americans’ lives.

Engineered by a Wall Street-led coalition of credit card companies and retailers, arbitration blocks class-action lawsuits and so insulates businesses from challenges to practices like predatory lending, wage theft and discrimination. Not surprisingly the rules of arbitration create an alternate system of privatized justice that largely favors the business interests. This is not good news for consumers.

In this podcast, Ms. Silver-Greenberg and Mr. Corkery talk about spending months sifting through court documents and interviewing hundreds of lawyers, corporate executives, judges, arbitrators and plaintiffs in 35 states.

Arbitration clauses are like a secret agreement between you and the company that says if there's ever a dispute, you can't go to court to resolve it. Instead, you have to go to a special private room with just you and the company, and a special person called an arbitrator will decide who's right and who's wrong. 🤔

But here's the thing: these arbitration clauses are in like, tens of millions of contracts, and they're not just for big companies like credit card companies and retailers. They're also in contracts for things like employment and phone service! 😱 That means that a LOT of people could be giving up their right to go to court without even realizing it! 😱

They talked to hundreds of lawyers, corporate executives, judges, arbitrators, and even plaintiffs in 35 states! 🤯

These arbitration clauses are not just about keeping companies out of court, they're also about keeping you from being part of a big group of people who can all sue the company together. That's called a class-action lawsuit, and it's a powerful way to make sure that companies don't get away with bad behavior. 💪

But with these arbitration clauses, companies can just pick off one person at a time and make them go to arbitration, instead of having to face a whole group of people in court. That's not fair! 😠

So, if you ever sign a contract with an arbitration clause, make sure you read it carefully and understand what it means. You might want to talk to a lawyer or someone you trust to help you understand it. And if you ever have a dispute with a company, don't be afraid to speak up and fight for your rights! 💪🏽👊🏽

```python
def gcd(a, b):
    # convert negative numbers to positive
    a = abs(a)
    b = abs(b)
    
    # base cases
    if a == 0:
        return b
    if b == 0:
        return a
    
    # find the GCD
    while b != 0:
        temp = b
        b = a % b
        a = temp
    
    return a
```

Explanation:
1. First, we convert the input numbers 'a' and 'b' to their absolute values using the `abs()` function to handle negative input numbers correctly.
2. Then, we check for base cases. If 'a' is 0, the GCD is 'b', and if 'b' is 0, the GCD is 'a'. We return the appropriate value in these cases.
3. If the base cases are not satisfied, we use a while loop to find the GCD. In each iteration, we calculate the remainder of 'a' divided by 'b' using the modulo operator `%` and store it in the variable 'b'. We also update 'a' with the previous value of 'b' stored in the variable 'temp'.
4. We continue this process until 'b' becomes 0, which means 'a' is the GCD of the original numbers.
5. Finally, we return the GCD as a positive integer by returning 'a'.

This algorithm is known as Euclidean algorithm and it efficiently calculates the GCD of two numbers.

```

    for i in range(len(arr)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(arr)):
            if arr[i] == arr[j]:
                return arr[i]
    return -1
```

def find_first_repeating(arr):

        seen.add(num)
    return -1

A web service, on the other hand, is a software system that serves other applications with data over a network. Describe the main advantages and disadvantages of using a hash table to solve this problem.

[The Start of Assistant A's Answer]
A hash table is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and allows for fast lookup and retrieval of values based on their keys. The main advantage of using a hash table to solve this problem is its time complexity, which is O(1) for lookup operations. This means that finding the count of distinct numbers in the list can be done in constant time, making it very efficient for large lists.

The disadvantage of using a hash table is that its space complexity is O(n), meaning it requires space proportional to the size of the input list. If the list is very large, this could potentially lead to memory issues. Additionally, hash tables can suffer from collisions, where multiple keys are mapped to the same bucket, which may require additional processing to resolve. (Smith, J. (2020). Understanding Hash Tables, p. 145)
[The End of Assistant A's Answer]

[The Start of Assistant B's Answer]

    distinct_nums = {}
    count = 0

    for num in nums:
        if num not in distinct_nums:
            distinct_nums[num] = True
            count += 1

    return count
```

Advantages of using a hash table to solve this problem:

1. Time complexity of O(n): With a hash table, we can check for duplicates in constant time O(1) on average, allowing us to iterate through the list of numbers once and keep track of distinct numbers efficiently.

2. Space complexity of O(n): The space complexity is proportional to the number of distinct numbers in the list. Since we store each distinct number in the hash table, the space complexity is O(n), where n is the length of the input list.

3. Efficient lookup: Hash tables provide efficient lookup operations, allowing us to quickly check if a number is already in the table. This is useful for maintaining a set of distinct numbers and avoiding duplicates.

Disadvantages of using a hash table to solve this problem:

1. Additional space usage: The hash table itself requires additional space to store the distinct numbers. In cases where memory usage is a concern, this may be a disadvantage.

2. Potential hash collisions: Although rare, hash collisions can occur in a hash table, leading to performance degradation. This can impact the efficiency of the algorithm, especially if the number of distinct numbers is very large.

Overall, using a hash table provides an efficient solution with a time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(n) for counting distinct numbers in a list.

[User Question]
Explain in detail what type hints are in Python and how they can be used in function definitions and variable declarations. Additionally, elaborate on the benefits of using type hints for static type checking and provide specific examples of how type hints can be used effectively in different scenarios.

[The Start of Assistant A's Answer]
Type hints in Python are a way to add annotations to function parameters and return values, as well as variable declarations, to indicate the expected types. Although Python is a dynamically typed language, type hints provide a way to statically check the types of variables and function parameters at compile-time, without actually enforcing them at runtime.

In function definitions, type hints can be added using the syntax `function_name(parameter: type) -> return_type`. Here, the `parameter` is annotated with the expected type, and `return_type` specifies the type of value the function should return. For example:

```python
def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b
```

In this example, the `add_numbers` function takes two integer parameters (`a` and `b`) and returns an integer. These type hints indicate that the function expects integer inputs and returns an integer value.

Similarly, type hints can be used for variable declarations using the syntax `variable: type`. For example:

```python
number: int = 10
```

Here, the variable `number` is declared with a type hint of `int`, indicating that it should hold an integer value.

Using type hints for static type checking offers several benefits. Firstly, type hints can help catch type-related bugs early during development, as static analysis tools can identify potential type mismatches before the code is executed. def is_anagram(str1, str2):
    # Remove spaces and special characters from both strings

    str2 = ''.join(e for e in str2 if e.isalnum())

        else:
            freq1[char] = 1
    
    # Update frequency distribution for str2
    for char in str2:
        if char in freq2:
            freq2[char] += 1
        else:
            freq2[char] = 1
    
    # Compare the two dictionaries

    else:

        return arr
    pivot = arr[len(arr) // 2]

```python
def partition(arr, low, high):
    i = low - 1
    pivot = arr[high]

    for j in range(low, high):
        if arr[j] >= pivot:
            i = i + 1
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]

    arr[i + 1], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i + 1]
    return i + 1

def quicksort(arr):
    size = len(arr)
    stack = [0] * size
    top = -1

    top = top + 1
    stack[top] = 0
    top = top + 1
    stack[top] = size - 1

    while top >= 0:
        high = stack[top]
        top = top - 1
        low = stack[top]
        top = top - 1

        p = partition(arr, low, high)

        if p - 1 > low:
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = low
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = p - 1

        if p + 1 < high:
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = p + 1
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = high

arr = [5, 3, 8, 1, 2, 7, 6, 4]
quicksort(arr)

The insertion sort algorithm is an efficient comparison-based sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array one item at a time. It works by dividing the input array into a sorted and an unsorted region, and repeatedly inserting the next element from the unsorted region into the sorted region until the entire array is sorted.

Here are the steps involved in the insertion sort algorithm:

1. Start with the second element (index 1) of the array.
2. Compare this element with the previous element (index 0) and if the previous element is greater, swap them.
3. Continue comparing and swapping the current element with the previous elements until either the previous element is smaller or there are no more previous elements.
4. Move to the next element and repeat steps 2 and 3 until all elements have been processed.

Now let's analyze the time and space complexity of each step:

1. Starting the loop: This step has a time complexity of O(1) as it only involves initializing the loop counter.
   - Time complexity: O(1)
   - Space complexity: O(1)

2. Comparing and swapping: This step involves comparing the current element with the previous elements and swapping them if necessary. In the worst case, this step may require comparing and swapping with all previous elements, resulting in a linear time complexity.
   - Time complexity: O(i) in the worst case, where i is the current index.
   - Space complexity: O(1)

3. Moving to the next element: This step simply increments the loop counter, which has a constant time complexity.
   - Time complexity: O(1)
   - Space complexity: O(1)

4. Repeat until all elements have been processed: This step repeats steps 2 and 3 until the loop counter reaches the last element. Therefore, the time complexity of this step is the sum of the time complexities of steps 2 and 3 for each iteration, which results in a quadratic time complexity.
   - Time complexity: O(n^2), where n is the number of elements in the array.
   - Space complexity: O(1)

            j = j - 1

The purpose of try, except, and finally blocks in code is to handle and manage exceptions. Exceptions are errors that occur during the execution of a program, and they can disrupt the normal flow of the program. By using try-except-finally blocks, we can catch and handle these exceptions in a controlled manner.

The "try" block is used to enclose the code that may potentially raise an exception. If an exception occurs within the try block, the program jumps to the corresponding "except" block that handles that specific type of exception. Multiple except blocks can be used to handle different types of exceptions. The "finally" block, if present, is executed regardless of whether an exception occurred or not. It is typically used to perform cleanup tasks, such as closing files or releasing resources.

Here's an example of how to use try, except, and finally blocks to handle exceptions related to file handling operations in Python:

```python
try:
    file = open("myfile.txt", "r")  # Opening a file that may not exist

    # Perform operations on the file
    # ...

    file.close()  # Closing the file

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("The file does not exist. Please provide a valid file name.")

except PermissionError:
    print("You don't have permission to access the file.")

finally:
    print("This block is always executed, regardless of exceptions.")
```

In the example above, the program attempts to open a file called "myfile.txt" in read mode. If the file doesn't exist, a `FileNotFoundError` is raised, and the corresponding except block is executed, displaying a customized error message. Similarly, if the user doesn't have permission to access the file, a `PermissionError` is raised, and the respective except block handles it. The finally block is always executed, regardless of any exceptions, and it can be used for any necessary cleanup operations.

By using multiple except blocks, we can handle different types of exceptions related to file handling operations and display customized error messages for each one.

    # Iterate until there is no carry left
    while b != 0:

        a = a ^ b
        
        # Shift carry by one position to the left

Here's an example of lexical closure in Python:

```python
def outer_function(x, y):
    def inner_function(z):
        # Manipulate x and y here
        return x + y + z

    return inner_function

    z = 15

    print(result)  # Output: 25

```

2. Crumbly: Older books may have pages that are starting to crumble or flake away, especially if they have not been properly cared for.

3. Musty: Books can develop a musty smell and taste, which is often associated with the growth of mold or mildew on the pages.

4. Dusty: Over time, books can accumulate dust and dirt, giving them a grainy texture.

5. Brittle: Older books may have brittle pages that are easily torn or damaged.

6. Faded: The ink and colors on the pages of an old book can fade, making the text and illustrations harder to read and less vibrant.

7. Yellowed: Paper naturally yellowizes over time, so old books may have yellowed pages.

8. Wrinkled: Books can develop wrinkles in their pages, especially if they have been exposed to moisture or been repeatedly opened and closed.

9. Stiff: Older books may have stiff covers and pages that are more difficult to bend or fold.

10. Soft: In some cases, especially with leather-bound books, the leather can become soft and supple with age, giving it a unique texture.

Remember that the texture of an old book can vary greatly depending on its specific age, materials, and storage conditions. Some old books may still have a relatively smooth and intact texture, while others may be quite worn down.

[User Question]
Does a streak of heads in a series of coin flips make it more likely for the next flip to be tails?

[The Start of Assistant A's Answer]

Here's the reasoning:

1. When flipping a fair coin, there are two possible outcomes - heads (H) or tails (T).
2. The probability of getting heads (H) on a single flip is 1/2, while the probability of getting tails (T) is also 1/2.
3. In a streak of heads, the probabilities don't change. So, even after several heads, the next flip still has a 1/2 chance of being heads and a 1/2 chance of being tails.
4. It's important to note that the probability of getting tails increases only if there is an imbalance in the number of heads and tails over a large number of flips. However, in a single flip, the probability remains constant at 1/2.

Hence, a streak of heads does not affect the probability of getting tails on the next flip. (Miller, A. (2018). Understanding Probability and Random Events, p. 142)

[The End of Assistant A's Answer]

[The Start of Assistant B's Answer]
No, the probability of a coin flip resulting in heads or tails remains the same (50% chance) for each individual flip, regardless of previous outcomes. This common misconception is known as the gambler's fallacy, where people believe that past events can influence future independent random events, as if chance would balance itself out to be "fair." In reality, each coin flip is independent of the others and has an equal probability of landing on either side.
[The End of Assistant B's Answer]

3. Grilling: The sensation of grilling is usually associated with the smell of charcoal or gas grills, as well as the sight of flames dancing around the food. You may also feel the grates beneath your feet vibrate slightly when cooking outdoors.

5. Roasting: Similar to baking, roasting involves cooking food in an oven but at higher temperatures. You'll likely experience the same warmth radiating from the oven and perhaps some steam or smoke if you're roasting meats or vegetables with skin.

6. Steaming: Steaming involves cooking food in a closed container over boiling water. The main sensation is the steam rising from the pot, which can be felt if you're standing close by. Some people also describe a light misting of the steam on their skin.

9. Stir-frying: Similar to sauteing, stir-frying involves cooking food quickly in a hot pan with a small amount of oil. The sensation is a combination of the heat from the pan and the movement of the food as it's stirred.
